lead: Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is a material extrusion additive process. A thermoplastic filament is pushed by drive rollers into a heated nozzle, melted, and laid as a thin road along a computer-controlled path. The bed lowers by one layer height and the next raster is deposited, so the part grows as a stack of layers. It exists because the machine is simple, clean and low-cost. It is used for prototypes, jigs, fixtures, teaching models and some end-use plastic parts. The standard family name is material extrusion; FDM is a trademark name.
prereq: You need: Chapter 7.2 for the STL-to-part chain, and Unit 3, Shaping of plastics: injection moulding and extrusion for polymer flow.

blocks.text: Material extrusion makes a part by forcing a melted polymer through a small nozzle. The feedstock is a solid filament, usually 1.75 mm or 2.85 mm diameter, wound on a spool. Two drive rollers grip the filament and push it. The nozzle is heated, so the polymer becomes a viscous melt. The nozzle moves in x and y over a build platform, called the bed. The bed moves down in z after each layer. The extruded road is called a raster. A layer is a set of parallel rasters, often at an angle to the previous layer.

items: Common filaments are PLA (polylactic acid), ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene), PETG (polyethylene terephthalate glycol), nylon and PEEK (polyether ether ketone).
PLA is easy to print and low-warp. ABS and PETG are tougher. Nylon is wear-resistant. PEEK is high-temperature and needs a hot nozzle and a heated chamber.
Load the filament, set nozzle and bed temperatures for the polymer, and home the axes.
Drive rollers feed filament into the heater; the melt leaves the nozzle as a road.
The slicer sets layer height h (mm), raster angle (degrees), infill (%) and support.
The nozzle traces the raster for one layer; the bed lowers by h; the next layer is deposited.
Remove support and post-process: trim, sand, anneal or vapour-smooth if needed.
Layer height h: vertical thickness of one layer, in mm.
Raster angle: direction of roads in a layer, in degrees from the x axis. Alternating 45° and 135° is common.
Infill: internal fill fraction, from 0% hollow to 100% solid.
Support: extra material under overhangs, removed after printing.

blocks.text: Bonds between roads and between layers form by cooling and polymer diffusion, not by melting the whole part. Strength is lower along z, so the part is anisotropic. Raster angle, layer height and nozzle temperature change strength. Nozzle diameter sets road width; layer height sets vertical step. They are not the same number.

Build time is estimated from the path length, not the solid volume. For a part with N layers, let L be the extruder path length in one layer in mm, and v the print speed in mm/s. Then T = N L / v. T is build time in s. This ignores travel between rasters, acceleration, layer changes and support. If support is used, add its path length to L. Layer height h sets vertical growth: total height = N h. A smaller h gives smoother walls but needs more layers, so build time rises. Infill changes L: 20% infill has a shorter path than 100% infill, but the outer walls and top layers still use solid roads. Print speed is limited by melt flow: too fast and the filament slips or the road is thin.

blocks.where: T is build time in s; N is number of layers; L is extruder path length in one layer in mm; v is print speed in mm/s. Add support path to L. Total height = N h, with h the layer height in mm.

examples.question: A FDM part has 100 layers, each of height 0.2 mm. The extruder path in each layer is 250 mm long and the print speed is 50 mm/s. Find the build time, ignoring travel, acceleration and layer-change time. Give the answer in seconds and minutes.
steps: Number of layers N = 100. Layer height h = 0.2 mm. Total height = N h = 100 × 0.2 = 20 mm.
Extruder path in one layer L = 250 mm.
Time for one layer t1 = L / v = 250 / 50 = 5 s.
Total build time T = N t1 = 100 × 5 = 500 s.
examples.answer: The build time is 500 s, that is 8.3333 min.
examples.check:
layers = 100
layer_height = 0.2
path_per_layer = 250
speed = 50
time_s = layers * path_per_layer / speed
time_min = time_s / 60
print(int(time_s))
print(round(time_min, 4))

traps: FDM is material extrusion, not sintering or curing. There is no laser, powder bed or resin vat.
Layer height is not nozzle diameter. Nozzle diameter sets road width; layer height sets the vertical step.
Part strength depends on raster angle and layer bonding. Do not use bulk polymer strength for a printed part.
The build-time formula T = N L / v ignores travel, acceleration, support and layer changes. Exams often add these.
Support is not infill. Support holds overhangs and is removed; infill stays inside the part.

quiz.q: What does FDM stand for, and what is the standard family name?
quiz.a: Fused deposition modelling; the standard family is material extrusion.

quiz.q: Why does the bed lower after each layer?
quiz.a: To keep the nozzle at the correct gap and place the next layer one layer height above the previous one; the part grows layer by layer.

quiz.q: A part has 80 layers. Each layer path is 180 mm and print speed is 60 mm/s. Find build time in seconds and minutes, ignoring travel.
Why is an FDM part often weaker in the z direction?
quiz.a: Layer interfaces bond by cooling and polymer diffusion; they have weaker chains than the bulk road. Loads across layers can open these bonds, so strength is anisotropic.

quiz.q: State the difference between layer height and nozzle diameter.
quiz.a: Layer height is the vertical thickness of one deposited layer. Nozzle diameter is the opening that sets the road width. A 0.4 mm nozzle can print a 0.1 mm layer.

quiz.q: A print uses 60 layers of 0.25 mm. What is the total height?
Why does 20% infill not make build time 20% of solid?
quiz.a: Outer walls, top and bottom layers remain solid, and the path includes perimeters. Infill only reduces the internal raster path. Travel and layer changes also add time.

quiz.q: Name two common FDM filaments and one high-temperature filament.
quiz.a: PLA and ABS are common; PEEK is high-temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial material extrusion now includes high-temperature machines for PEEK and ULTEM, heated chambers, and continuous fibre reinforcement. Printers use sensor feedback and automatic bed levelling. Research focuses on interlayer bonding, warpage and anisotropic design. Search for fused filament fabrication, material extrusion, raster angle and interlayer strength.
